newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria conservatives warn Klima on CA.
newsitem.headline: Austria conservatives warn Klima on CA.

text.p: The conservative People's Party on Monday demanded urgent legal changes to prevent Bank Austria winning the bid in the long-running privatisation saga of Austria's flagship bank Creditanstalt.

The People's Party (OeVP), junior partners in a coalition with Social Democrats, called for an emergency session of parliament early in the New Year in a last ditch attempt to push through legislation changing the law on privatisation and floatations.
"Finance Minister Viktor Klima would be well advised to wait so that he does not take any steps he might regret later," OeVP chairman Andreas Khol told a news conference.

Tension has been high in the government coalition since "socialist" Bank Austria entered the fray for the sale of conservative stronghold Creditanstalt-Bankverein shortly before the original December 16 deadline for bids.

Klima late on Friday reopened the tender for the sale of the government's 70 percent stake in Austria's second biggest bank to give current bidders more time to improve their offers, setting a new deadline for January 10, 1997.

Khol said his party's main priority was to see the bank floated on the Vienna bourse with part of the stock distributed to employees. Selling Creditanstalt to Bank Austria would be a "glaring breach of the coalition agreement", Khol noted.
The conservatives were prepared to join forces with other parties to win the necessary majority in parliament against the Social Democrats, he said. Such a move could lead to a government collapse.

The conservatives and the Social Democrats fell out in a budget row in October 1995, forcing a snap general election in December of the same year just 14 months after the last nationwide poll. The two parties resumed their 10-year coalition partnership but relations have remained strained, particularly over economic policy.

Bank Austria, effectively controlled by Social Democrat-dominated City of Vienna, is up against rival offers from a consortium led by Austro-Italian insurer EA Generali, favoured by the conservatives, and Austrian entrepreneur Karl Wlaschek, an outsider.
Bank Austria has made an offer of 836 schillings per share for the whole of the government's stake in Creditanstalt, amounting to a total of 16.7 billion schillings ($1.53 billion).
The state's holding is worth 14.5 billion schillings at market prices.

The consortium has offered 730 schillings per share for 14.7 million shares and 580 schillings for the remaining 5.2 million shares, which it plans to float on the stock market, according to the finance ministry.
The bid by unfancied Wlaschek was not disclosed but is estimated around 15 billion schillings.
The far right Freedom Party has threatened to bring a vote of no confidence against Klima if he does not sell the bank to the highest bidder, as stipulated by European Union law.
